entries.clue: Perhaps selfie after selfie, ultimately overblown (4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means at the very end, so only the letter the word finishes on is wanted.
indicatorNotes.after: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the piece named first in the clue ends up second.

blocks.note: the letter the word selfie ends on
a selfie is one kind of pic, the informal shortening of picture, and 'perhaps' flags it as an example

annotation.surface: Somebody posting one selfie after another until the whole performance gets out of hand.
annotation.walkthrough: One word serves twice over, which is why the clue reads like a repetition of itself. 'Overblown' looks like a verdict on the photographs and is in fact the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Something epic is on a heroic scale, and used of a performance that scale tips over into the overblown.

entries.clue: Pink geese, barking dog (9)

indicatorNotes.barking: Barking is British slang for completely mad, and letters treated madly will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: A farmyard of pink geese with a dog making a racket among them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Barking' is placed to sound like the noise the dog is making and is doing the shuffling instead — British English uses it for stark madness, as in barking mad. The breed keeps the old spelling of Beijing.
annotation.definitionFit: A Pekingese is the small flat-faced lap dog bred in the Chinese imperial palace, so 'dog' names it by species.

entries.clue: Joined overthrow of government – then governed (7)

blocks.note: a coup is the sudden seizure of power from a sitting government
whoever led the country governed it

annotation.surface: Generals who took part in toppling a government and then ran the country themselves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Joined' opens the clue looking like a verb describing the plotters, and it is the definition standing outside the wordplay. The dash marks the seam between the two chunks.
annotation.definitionFit: To be coupled is to be joined in a pair — railway carriages, dancers, ideas — so 'joined' is the same word in the same past tense.

entries.clue: Also one of Disney+’s characters (4)

blocks.note: the little word that adds one thing on to another, as in 'two and two'
the symbol printed at the end of the streaming service's name, read as a piece of type rather than a cartoon

annotation.surface: Naming one more of the cartoon characters on Disney's streaming channel.
annotation.walkthrough: Disney's characters are Mickey and Goofy until you notice that a character is also a printed symbol, and that the brand name ends in one. Four letters is what forces the second reading.
annotation.definitionFit: Plus is the conjunction meaning also, and it is the name of the + sign that finishes the brand Disney+.

entries.clue: Like young wizard’s bowls and plates? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: Pottery is a mass noun naming the whole class of fired clay ware, so a plural pair of examples is the natural way to point at it.

blocks.note: Harry Potter, the schoolboy wizard of the novels; the possessive belongs to the surface only
the adjective ending -y means resembling, and it is a single letter

annotation.surface: Wondering whether the crockery on the table belongs to the boy wizard.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Like' looks like the start of a comparison and is really a suffix, waiting at the front of the clue for the name it attaches to. The question mark admits that bowls and plates are examples rather than a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: Pottery is fired earthenware, which is what household bowls and plates are made as, so the definition names the class by two of its members.

entries.clue: Taking slices of charcuterie – we’ve all been there (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a joke about the answer rather than a synonym for it: it names the place by the one visit every reader has made, and its plural matches the many of us.

indicatorNotes.Taking slices of: A slice is cut out of something bigger, so a piece of the word that follows is taken and the rest left behind.

blocks.note: five letters in an unbroken run, starting at the U in the middle of the word

annotation.surface: Cutting slices off a platter of cold meats, something everyone has done.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman likes a long imported word as a hiding place: charcuterie is read as a thing on a board, not as a row of letters. The run sits inside one word rather than across a join, which makes it harder to see.
annotation.definitionFit: A uterus is the womb, and every person spent nine months inside one, which is the shared experience the clue points at.

entries.clue: American-European union welcomed by Florida as advantageous (6)

indicatorNotes.welcomed by: Somebody welcomed by a host is taken inside the house, so that letter sits within the pair that follows.

blocks.note: US is the standard short form for American
e is the standard abbreviation for European
FL is Florida's two-letter postal code
u is the standard abbreviation for union

annotation.surface: Florida glad to take in a transatlantic partnership and finding that it pays.
annotation.walkthrough: 'American-European union' reads as one alliance and is three separate pieces, the last of them the union that goes indoors. US state codes are fair material in British crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: Something useful serves a purpose and is worth having, which is what 'advantageous' says of anything that works in your favour.

entries.clue: Inventor facing the wrong way: side on (6)

indicatorNotes.facing the wrong way: Something facing the wrong way has been turned about, so its letters are read from the far end back.

blocks.note: the four letters of SIDE written from the back
the two letters stand exactly as printed

annotation.surface: An inventor photographed back to front and in profile.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Side on' is an everyday phrase for in profile, and the clue needs it as two separate pieces — the colon is what disguises the split. Only the first of the two turns round.
annotation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison patented the phonograph and the first practical light bulb, so 'inventor' names him by the trade he is famous for.

entries.clue: Spooner’s to cycle past Royal Courts of Justice? Let’s hear some music (6,2,3,4)

indicatorNotes.Spooner’s: Spooner was the Oxford don famous for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so those two openings change places.

blocks.note: To cycle is to bike. That word hands its B over to the other one and takes back the STR coming the other way.
to ride past a building on a London street is to go up the street it stands on
The Royal Courts of Justice stand on the Strand in central London. The street name gives up its STR, collects the B, and keeps its 'the'.

annotation.surface: The Reverend Spooner describing a bike ride up past the London law courts.
annotation.walkthrough: The address is the whole clue: the Royal Courts of Justice sit on the Strand, the street running east from Trafalgar Square, and 'up the Strand' is how Londoners say it. Say that, then trade the two openings.
annotation.definitionFit: To strike up the band is to have the music start, so 'let's hear some music' is the same call in plain words.

entries.clue: Criticise King Edward for one having beef with this? (5,6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition works by company rather than by synonym, and its participle stands where a noun would: the thing you have beef with is the thing named.

blocks.note: to roast somebody is to criticise them mercilessly
a King Edward is one of Britain's best-known varieties of the vegetable, and 'for one' flags it as an example

annotation.surface: A monarch being taken to task by somebody who has a grievance with him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beef' is the pivot: the surface wants the idiom for a quarrel, and the plate wants the meat. 'King Edward' is a potato here before he is a king.
annotation.definitionFit: A roast potato is what shares the plate with roast beef at a British Sunday lunch, so the clue names it by the company it keeps.

entries.clue: Acid satire represented a part of the Med (8,3)

indicatorNotes.represented: To re-present something is to set it out afresh, so the same letters are laid down again in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters
the article joins the fodder and makes eleven

annotation.surface: A biting satirical piece that stood for somewhere in the Mediterranean.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Represented' has a hyphen hiding in it — re-presented, set out again — and that is the whole instruction. 'The Med' is the everyday British short form for the Mediterranean.
annotation.definitionFit: The Adriatic Sea is the long arm of the Mediterranean between Italy and the Balkans, so 'part of the Med' places it rather than naming it.

entries.clue: Principally, facecloth (literally); alternatively, nicey nicey eulogising laudation? (7)

annotation.definition: Principally, facecloth (literally); alternatively, nicey nicey eulogising laudation?

indicatorNotes.Principally: Principally points at what comes first, so each word in the list gives up only the letter it opens with.

blocks.clueFragment: facecloth (literally); alternatively, nicey nicey eulogising laudation
blocks.note: seven words in the order printed, each handing over the letter it starts with

annotation.surface: A dictionary entry offering a word's plain meaning first and its sugary one second.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is made of the very stuff it describes: a pile of words for empty praise is flannel itself. In Britain a flannel is the small cloth kept by the basin for washing your face.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is both senses at once: literally the facecloth, and figuratively the soft-soaping talk that flatters while saying nothing.

entries.clue: Result of rogue régimes? (7)

indicatorNotes.rogue: A rogue thing has gone off on its own, out of the order it was put in, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: seven letters to be rearranged; the French accent counts for nothing

annotation.surface: A question about what lawless governments leave behind them.
annotation.walkthrough: Definition and wordplay are the same seven letters, so nothing is left over to point at the answer — the whole sentence does that job. Everyman keeps the French accents that both the fodder and the answer carry in print.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is what a rogue régime produces: the people who leave the country because of it.

entries.clue: Duke wearing beam following frothy coffee: how modern! (6-3)

indicatorNotes.wearing: What you wear goes round the outside of you, so the piece named before it ends up inside the piece named after it.
indicatorNotes.following: To follow is to come along behind, so everything named before it lands second in the answer.

blocks.note: a latte is the milky coffee, frothed on top
a beam of light is a ray
d is the standard abbreviation for duke
surface padding: the exclamation dresses the definition up as a remark

annotation.surface: A duke in a spotlight with a cappuccino, offered as a picture of modern life.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon is the seam — everything in front of it spells, and the exclamation behind it defines. D for duke is one of the single-letter abbreviations worth learning early.
annotation.definitionFit: A latter-day version of something is its present-day one, so 'modern' is the same adjective doing the same job in front of a noun.

entries.clue: Depicted as haggard (5)

blocks.note: what a pencil or a pen has done to put a thing on paper
of a face: pulled tight and hollowed out by strain or illness

annotation.surface: A portrait that shows its sitter looking careworn.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same past participle, joined by nothing but 'as'. The senses meet at the idea of pulling: a line pulled across paper, a face pulled thin by strain.
annotation.definitionFit: Something drawn has been depicted in line, and a face drawn by illness or worry looks haggard — one participle, one from the pencil and one from the strain.

entries.clue: Old Spanish coins criminally unsold? Boo (9)

indicatorNotes.criminally: To do a thing criminally is to do it wrongly, and letters put down wrongly are letters out of their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters, the jeer included

annotation.surface: Outrage that the stock has gone unsold, and a jeer thrown at the news.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman often ends a clue with an interjection, and the temptation is to read it as comment rather than material. Doubloons are pirate treasure because Spain shipped its American gold home across the Caribbean.
annotation.definitionFit: A doubloon was the gold coin of the Spanish empire, minted for three centuries, so the definition names the currency by nation and era.

entries.clue: Thieved a gown (5)

blocks.note: the past tense of the verb to steal
in its oldest sense a long robe reaching to the feet, later the wrap worn over the shoulders

annotation.surface: Somebody made off with a dress.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words, and two of them are definitions — about the shortest shape a cryptic clue comes in. The garment sense is old: a Roman stola was a full-length robe before the word narrowed to a priest's or a woman's shoulder wrap.
annotation.definitionFit: Stole is the past tense of steal, and a stole is the long robe or shoulder wrap the clue's second half is after.

entries.clue: Formality that’s found in toast (6)

blocks.note: stiffness of manner, the figurative use of a stiffened collar
the carbohydrate that makes up most of a slice of bread

annotation.surface: The stiffness that settles over a dinner where glasses are being raised.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Toast' is the trap — the raised glass, not the grilled bread — and only the bread has the substance in it. Laundry starch stiffens a collar, which is how the word came to describe a manner.
annotation.definitionFit: Starch stiffens a shirt collar, and that stiffness is what 'formality' names in a person's manner; it is also the carbohydrate a slice of toast is mostly made of.

entries.clue: Describing silvery metal, irritated Marie Curie twice cut off by lecturer (9)

indicatorNotes.irritated: Somebody irritated is stirred up, and stirred-up letters come out in a different order.
indicatorNotes.twice cut off: To cut a word off is to take away the letter at its end, and doing it twice takes the next one back as well.

blocks.note: the ten letters of the name with the last two taken off the end
l is the standard abbreviation for lecturer

annotation.surface: An annoyed Marie Curie being interrupted twice by a lecturer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut off' reads as an interruption rather than an instruction, and the docking happens before the letters are shuffled. Marie Curie never worked on mercury — radium and polonium were hers — so the name is material, not a hint.
annotation.definitionFit: Mercurial is the adjective belonging to mercury, the liquid silvery metal, even though its everyday use is about changeable temper.

entries.clue: Grammar queen ignored to some extent in exhibition venue (7)

indicatorNotes.ignored to some extent: What is ignored is passed over, and only some of it — so letters drop off each end and the unbroken middle is what remains.

blocks.note: seven letters in an unbroken row, picked up midway through the first word and stopping just short of the end of the second

annotation.surface: A stickler for grammar being half-ignored at a trade fair.
annotation.walkthrough: The hiding place straddles the gap between the two words, which is where these runs are hardest to see. Everyman's usual signal is a word of quantity, and here the quantity is attached to 'ignored' instead.
annotation.definitionFit: A marquee is the large tent hired for shows, fairs and receptions, so 'exhibition venue' names it by the job it is put up to do.

entries.clue: Mike ran madly to get little baking dish (7)

indicatorNotes.madly: To do something madly is to do it with no order at all, so the letters arrive in none.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: Mike sprinting like a lunatic to fetch a small dish.
annotation.walkthrough: A first name plus a short verb is the classic seven-letter anagram, and 'Mike' is also the radio alphabet's M — worth ruling out before you commit to the whole name. The dish is the one a crème brûlée is baked in.
annotation.definitionFit: A ramekin is the small straight-sided dish a soufflé or a crème brûlée is baked and served in.

entries.clue: They’re fatty muscular flaps: Everyman had tucked in (6)

annotation.definitionNote: Lipids are fats rather than fatty things, so the adjective stands in for a plural noun, with 'they're' doing the agreeing.

indicatorNotes.tucked in: Something tucked in has been pushed down inside whatever surrounds it, so those letters go within the other piece.

blocks.note: the two muscular folds round the mouth
Everyman speaks of himself as I, and 'had' contracts to 'd

annotation.surface: Everyman calling lips fatty flaps, having just eaten well.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tucked in' is how a British diner describes setting about a meal, and it is the insertion too. Everyman means himself whenever he signs his name inside a clue, and for spelling purposes that is an I.
annotation.definitionFit: Lipids are the fats and oils of living tissue, body fat among them, so 'fatty' names them by the one quality they all share.

entries.clue: Head of Anatomy to regret tartan cap – flipping unprofessional (7)

indicatorNotes.Head of: The head of a word is the letter it begins with, so one letter is all that is taken.
indicatorNotes.flipping: To flip a thing is to turn it right over, so the letters it governs are read the other way about.

blocks.note: the letter the word Anatomy starts with
to rue something is to regret it
a tam is the flat woollen Scottish bonnet, short for tam-o'-shanter and often woven in tartan

annotation.surface: The head of the anatomy department regretting a tartan cap and calling it flipping unprofessional.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is exactly the mild British oath a grumbling professor would reach for, which is what hides the instruction to read backwards. The bonnet takes its name from Burns's Tam o' Shanter.
annotation.definitionFit: An amateur does a thing for love rather than money, so 'unprofessional' here means unpaid rather than sloppy.

entries.clue: Tree you might turn to for advice (5)

annotation.definition2: you might turn to for advice

blocks.note: the small white-flowered tree of British hedgerows, cropped for cordial and for wine

blocks.clueFragment: you might turn to for advice
blocks.note: the senior member of a village, a church or a family, whose word carries weight

annotation.surface: A tree worth consulting when you need guidance.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it is a tree giving counsel, which is nonsense and is meant to be: the two halves are separate definitions with nothing joining them. Elderflowers and elderberries both come off it.
annotation.definitionFit: The elder is the hedgerow tree that gives elderflowers and elderberries, and an elder of a church or village is the senior figure whose advice is sought.

entries.clue: Namby-pamby takes money from old prince (7)

blocks.note: to milk somebody is to draw money out of them steadily
o is the standard abbreviation for old
p is the standard abbreviation for prince

annotation.surface: A weakling steadily fleecing an elderly prince.
annotation.walkthrough: Two of the seven letters come from single-letter abbreviations sitting in plain sight as an adjective and a noun, which is the hardest sort to notice. A milksop is literally bread soaked in milk, and that is where the insult comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: A milksop is a feeble, spiritless man, and 'namby-pamby' is the same insult used as a noun.

entries.clue: Loud coo and cluck up here? (5-6-4)

annotation.definition: Loud coo and cluck up here?

indicatorNotes.up: Something mixed up is out of its arrangement, and that is what has happened to the letters in front of it.

blocks.note: fifteen letters, every one of them used

annotation.surface: Birdsong from somewhere overhead, loud enough to be worth remarking on.
annotation.walkthrough: Aristophanes' birds built their city up in the clouds, which is where the phrase for a fool's paradise comes from. The italics do no work beyond marking the two bird noises.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is the place itself: the imaginary country up in the sky where birds coo and cluck, and where anyone with impossible hopes is said to live.

entries.clue: Quick – cut French cheese (4)

indicatorNotes.cut: A word that is cut is shortened, and what comes off is the letter at its end.

blocks.note: the adjective meaning quick or hurried, minus the F it ends on

annotation.surface: An order to hurry up and cut the cheese.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as somebody hurrying a cheeseboard along, which is why 'cut' looks like slicing rather than shortening. Brie is a district east of Paris, and the cheese carries its name.
annotation.definitionFit: Brie is the soft white-rinded cheese made east of Paris, so the definition names it by country and kind.

entries.clue: In hearing, is conscious of sensory organ (4)

indicatorNotes.In hearing: What is in hearing has reached the ear, so the words are wanted for the sound they make and not for their spelling.

blocks.note: to be conscious of something is to know it, and that verb's third person carries a silent K at the front

annotation.walkthrough: The silent K is the whole of it: said aloud, the verb for being aware and the organ are one noise. English keeps that K in writing only, a leftover from the Old English cnāwan.
annotation.definitionFit: The nose is the organ of smell, so 'sensory organ' names it by the sense it serves.
